checks.note: Both works exist (from recall). The data processing inequality I(X;Z)<=I(X;Y) for a Markov chain is stated in Cover & Thomas, not in Shannon 1948 as such. checks.note: From recall (pp. 1491-1501). The paper proposes N-version programming for fault tolerance. The product-of-p_i formula is just what independence would give; the paper argues for design diversity but does not guarantee independence, as the next entries show.

From recall (pp. 34-41); introduces mutation testing and the coupling-effect hypothesis. The 'checker cannot tell planted from real' assumption is the author's addition, not the paper's.

Confirmed via the USENIX listing (Dec 2011, vol 36 no 6) and a summary of the paper. It argues for treating inputs as languages, keeping them simple, and recognising fully before processing. It is a design principle, not a guarantee that the processor never acts on unrecognised input; recognising complex languages can be undecidable.

result.overall: All 23 sources exist and the bibliographic details are right. Only three records were confirmed by web search this session (RFC 9413, the LangSec ;login: paper, Eick et al. 1992); the rest rest on my recall of standard records, so treat them as unfetched. The main issues are attribution and overclaiming. The data processing inequality comes from the Cover & Thomas textbook, not Shannon 1948, and the 'product of retentions' bound is not a consequence of it. Merkle 1987 gives hash trees, not content addressing. LangSec and RFC 9413 are design arguments, not guarantees. Meyer's precondition is checked at callee entry, not at the call site.
